newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU official heads for S.Africa trade talks with open mind.
newsitem.headline: EU official heads for S.Africa trade talks with open mind.

text.p: The European Commission said on Wednesday it was going into important trade talks with South Africa this week with an open mind but warned of tough negotiations ahead.

"We are at the beginning of a complicated negotiating process but you must remember it is just that -- a negotiating process," said Philippe Soubestre, head of the European Commission's department responsible for development issues.
"I know of no comments, no papers or no objections (from the South Africans)," he said. "When I arrive I want to hear first-hand from them."

Soubestre, talking to reporters on the eve of departure for Johannesburg, said he understood the strength of feeling in South Africa for a "good trade deal", but that people should understand that negotiation was a two-way process.

"This process creates feelings on both sides and clearly from intitial positions there are differences of substance," he said. "But I don't know if the mood on the South African side represents all the nuances of the agreement we are aiming for."

Soubestre was speaking a day after South Africa's ambassador to the EU, Eltie Links, urged the Commission to radically rethink its approach to trade negotiations, saying Pretoria wanted "asymmetrical" trade liberalisation.

The EU has rejected South Africa's proposal for full accession to the Lome Convention which grants favourable access to EU markets to mainly former colonies of EU countries which are now developing nations in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific.
In its mandate presented last March, the EU suggested instead that both sides phase out certain tariff barriers over a 10-year period to create a free-trade area.

Faizel Ismail, director of foreign trade relations in South Africa's department of trade and industry, said on Tuesday that Pretoria's preference was for a trade and development agreement rather than a free trade agreement, since this would recognise developmental needs and the needs of the region.

Soubestre said, however, that the EU already "significantly addressed the development needs of South Africa", pointing out that the EU has already pledged 500 million European currency units ($594 million) in aid and the European Investment Bank a further 150 million Ecus.
"We don't decide on our own how this money should be spent," he said. "We want to hear from South Africa on their suggestions."
Soubestre said the EU was offering, in effect, duty-free access to the largest market in the world to 96 percent of South Africa's exports.
"Is this something South Africa is interested in, or not?" he asked. "Is this something South African businesses would be interested in, or not?"
Some 40 percent of South Africa's exports go to EU member states and more than one third of its imports are of EU origin. ($1=.8425 European Currency Unit)
